title: Tensor decomposition over an etale localization
statement: Let $A\to C$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings such that $C$ is free over $A$ with a finite basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Let $h\in C$, put $B=C_h$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], and assume that $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is etale [def-weil-affine-spectrum], [def-weil-etale-morphism]. Form the commutative algebra $T=C\otimes_A B$ [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property], regarded as a $B$-algebra through the second factor, and let $\mu:T\to B$ be the $B$-algebra map $c\otimes b\mapsto\bar c b$, where $\bar c$ is the image of $c$ in $B$. There exist a commutative $B$-algebra $D$ and an isomorphism of $B$-algebras $\theta:T\xrightarrow{\sim}B\times D$ such that $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\theta=\mu$.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the multiplication map C tensor_A C_h to C_h is etale and flat; Tag 00U8 (algebra.tex, lemma-surjective-flat-finitely-presented), applied there after Tag 00U7 (lemma-map-between-etale), gives the displayed product decomposition.

proof.text: Write $\lambda:C\to B$ for localization and $i:C\to T$, $j:B\to T$ for $c\mapsto c\otimes1$, $b\mapsto1\otimes b$. The tensor pushout universal property [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property](2) applied to $\lambda$ and $\mathrm{id}_B$ gives $\mu(c\otimes b)=\lambda(c)b$. It gives $\mu i=\lambda$ and $\mu j=\mathrm{id}_B$. In particular $\mu$ is surjective, and it is a $B$-algebra map for the second-factor structure $j$.

source.place: Tag 0812 (lemma-trick-fitting-ideal), proof: the multiplication map is a section; tensor formulas expanded

proof.text: Base change the assumed etale map $A\to B$ along $A\to C$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-ring-base-change], $\operatorname{Spec}T\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ induced by $i$ is etale. By [lem-weil-pbc-principal-localization-open-immersion], $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ induced by $\lambda$ is an open immersion, hence etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-composition-cancellation](1). For $f=\operatorname{Spec}\mu$ and $g=\operatorname{Spec}i$, the identity $\mu i=\lambda$ of Step 1 gives $g\circ f=\operatorname{Spec}\lambda$. Since $g$ and $g\circ f$ are etale, clause (3) of the same cancellation node implies that $f$ is etale. Thus $\mu:T\to B$ is a surjective ring map whose spectrum morphism is etale. This concerns $\mu$, not a claim that $T$ is etale as a $B$-algebra.

source.place: Tag 0812 proof, etaleness of the multiplication map; Algebra Tag 00U7 (lemma-map-between-etale), with base change 00U2 and principal localization 01I3

proof.text: Put $I=\ker\mu$. Steps 1-2 verify precisely the surjectivity and spectrum-etaleness assumptions of [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-etale-kernel-idempotent-fg], so $I^2=I$ and $I$ is finitely generated as an ideal of $T$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fg-idempotent-ideal-idempotent-generator](1) in the commutative ring $T$ to choose $e\in T$ with $e^2=e$ and $I=eT$. Since $e\in I$, $\mu(e)=0$. Set $q=1-e$; then $q^2=q$, $eq=0$, $q+e=1$, and $\mu(q)=1$.

Define $D=eT=\{et:t\in T\}$, with inherited addition and multiplication and identity $e$. It is a commutative ring: $e(et)=et$ and $(et)(eu)=e(tu)$, so these operations close in $D$. Give it the $B$-algebra structure $b\mapsto ej(b)$; this map preserves $1$ because the identity of $D$ is $e$. The map $\theta:T\to B\times D$, $t\mapsto(\mu(t),et)$, preserves addition and multiplication, since $e^2=e$, and preserves the identity $(1,e)$. It is a $B$-algebra map since $\theta(j(b))=(b,ej(b))$. Its first projection is $\mu$ by the displayed formula.

source.place: Tag 0812 proof, product splitting from 00U8; elementary complementary-idempotent product map written out

proof.text: For $(b,d)\in B\times D$, regarded with $d\in T$, set $\psi(b,d)=qj(b)+d$. Since $d\in eT=\ker\mu$, one has $\mu(d)=0$ and $ed=d$. Hence $\theta(\psi(b,d))=(b,d)$ using $\mu(q)=1$, $\mu j=\mathrm{id}_B$, and $eq=0$. Conversely, for $t\in T$ the element $t-j\mu(t)$ lies in $\ker\mu=eT$, so $q(t-j\mu(t))=0$. Therefore $qj\mu(t)=qt$ and $\psi(\theta(t))=qt+et=t$. These two identities show that $\theta$ is bijective, so the $B$-algebra map of Step 4 is the required $B$-algebra isomorphism, with $\operatorname{pr}_1\theta=\mu$.
